acceptance: A fixture imports a 200-line price book CSV with costs and markups, raises one category by 5%, quotes a flat-rate task and a time-and-materials line, and checks prices, costs and the round-trip export.

Its price is fixed, or follows its category's markup: unit cost × (100 + markup) / 100, rounded half up to the cent, recomputed whenever the cost or the markup changes.

A price-book quote line keeps the item's unit cost when it was priced.

title: Leads from Google, Angi, Thumbtack and Yelp
acceptance: A fixture posts a recorded lead payload from each provider (provider fakes), finds four requests with sources and lead costs, one matched to an existing customer, and an acknowledgment queued for each; a workflow rule on requests from Angi applies its lead cost (`API-005`).
Only the owner connects a lead source (lead connect action), with how many minutes the business has to acknowledge its leads (5 to 1,440, default 60) and the acknowledgment text.

Angi and Thumbtack post each lead (Thumbtack's Partner API v4 NegotiationCreatedV4 body; Angi's CRM lead delivery) to the source-specific lead receiver, and Yelp posts a notice naming new leads to the Yelp notice receiver, which Glove reads from Yelp's Leads API with the owner's key; Google Local Services has no push, so Glove reads the last week's leads from the Google Ads API (the provider’s service-lead record) with the owner's OAuth credentials and developer token on every scheduled run (every 15 minutes) and when the desk chooses **Read new leads** (lead pull action), and a failed scheduled read is a provider fact in Activity.
Google reads every response page with the same query and the provider's next-page token; repeated tokens, malformed rows or a failed later page refuse that entire read before requests are written.
Scheduled and desk retries retain one request per provider lead ID.

The posting doors authenticate before reading the body, as `COMM-001, COMM-010, COMM-011, COMM-012, COMM-013, COMM-014, COMM-015, COMM-016, COMM-017, COMM-018`'s unsigned callbacks do: HTTPS Basic user glove with a per-source password of 32 random bytes shown only in the connecting owner's response and kept as its SHA-256 hash (compared in constant time; reconnecting replaces it at once); every credential or form failure answers the same 401 body, writes nothing, and after 20 rejections from one address in a minute 429; a lead older than 7 days is refused, and a lead already landed (by provider and provider lead ID) lands nothing again.
Basic door passwords are stored only as SHA-256 hashes; provider keys are installation-local values in the installation-private provider store, with no sealed or encrypted storage claim.
Both stay out of records, Activity, command outcomes, the export and the archive.

title: Service calls booked without a quote
acceptance: A fixture takes a phoned-in request for a leaking water heater, creates a job with an $89.00 diagnostic fee from the price book, books it for today, and the technician adds a flat-rate valve replacement and 1.5 hours of labor on site with the customer's approval; the invoice draft carries exactly the fee, both lines and the recorded materials, and is approved and invoiced; a browser journey creates the same kind of job from the customer record.

The dispatcher, the office or the owner makes a service call (job create action without a quote) from a request (which is then won) or from the customer record, at one of that customer's sites, with zero or more lines from the price book or custom; its checklist and forms come from those lines as for a quoted job.
Its timeline says it was made without a quote, its screen shows no accepted price, and its booking, field capture and completion are any job's.

On site the assigned technician adds work only on a service call (on a quoted job that is a change order, `QUOTE-006, QUOTE-016, QUOTE-017, QUOTE-018`): a price-book item other than a material, a quantity, and the customer's approval (their name, and signed on the phone or told in person), queued through the phone's outbox; the technician sees no prices.

The invoice draft carries the job's lines, then the added work and the recorded price-book materials at today's price-book prices, so the office prices them by preparing, revising and approving the invoice under `GLOVE-09`; until that approval none of the job's prices counts as approved.

title: Discounts on quotes and invoices
acceptance: A fixture quotes parts of $400.00 (taxable at 8.25%) and labor of $300.00 (non-taxable) with a $50.00 non-taxable first-time-customer discount line and a 10% document discount, and checks subtotal $650.00, discount $65.00 taken from labor, tax $33.00 and total $618.00; a 50% document discount on the same lines spills $75.00 onto the parts and gives tax $26.81 and total $351.81; the accepted figures are identical to the cent on the job, the invoice, the CSV and the explicitly mapped QuickBooks inspection payload.
A discount line is a line whose unit price is negative (-50.00), custom or from a price-book item of kind discount (a fixed negative price, no cost); its line total rounds half a cent away from zero.
Each line is taxable or non-taxable as `MONEY-001, MONEY-004, MONEY-005` decides (item flag, labor rule, exemption); discount lines may not take either pool below zero.

The document discount is a percent of the subtotal (above 0 to 100, two places, amount rounded half up to the cent) or a fixed dollar amount, never above the subtotal, with a reason up to 100 characters.

It comes off the non-taxable lines first (line order, each line at most its own amount), then taxable lines in line order; tax is the jurisdiction rate on the remaining taxable cents, rounded half up once, and the total is subtotal − discount + tax.

Each quote option carries its own discount; add-ons take discount lines only; on acceptance the chosen option's discount applies to the accepted lines (a percent re-applies to their subtotal, an amount stays fixed).
The job and invoice carry it; an invoice revision or correction keeps it unless the payload sets another.

The CSV writes the discount as up to two rows (non-taxable and taxable amounts); the QuickBooks inspection payload writes a DiscountLineDetail with tax after discount and both amounts in its description; revenue reports and job costing use subtotal less discount.

title: Arrival windows and automatic assignment
acceptance: A fixture books three online requests and checks each lands on an eligible technician inside its window, then the dispatcher reassigns one with a `GLOVE-07` review; an assessment on a request is booked with its arrival window.

The planned start must fall inside the window, both ends included; otherwise the booking is refused.
Visit change action keeps the visit's window unless it names a new one, and removing the window removes it; a move whose planned start leaves the kept window is refused.
The window shows in the booking event ("9:00 AM – 10:30 AM (arrival window 8:00 AM – 10:00 AM)"), on the dispatcher's visit panel and on the technician's phone.

title: Message outcomes and customer warnings
acceptance: A message record keeps its kind, subject, recipient, from-address, provider and who sent it, never the body, so a booking link's bearer exists only in the email and the one-time command response.
After the command commits, Glove makes one send attempt with the message id as the delivery id.

The provider's answer (accepted, refused, rate limited or not confirmed) and every authenticated event the provider posts to the mail callback (delivered, deferred, bounced, complained, failed, rejected) are provider facts on the message's timeline, in Activity and in the business export with the provider's reference; Glove authenticates each callback under the rules below (using Base's verifier for SendGrid/Resend), and Base's durable store keeps each matched event once, and applies an event only to a message Glove sent through that provider to exactly that recipient; authenticated unmatched events return 200 without effect.

A message's state is the latest of its facts in Base's order: a final fact (delivered, bounced, complained, failed, rejected) is never replaced by a non-final one, and a later final fact (a complaint after delivery) replaces an earlier one. "Delivered" means the recipient's mail server accepted it, as the provider reported; Glove never claims a person read it.
Each failure shows on the message with what to do next.

A customer whose latest finished email to an address on their record bounced or was marked as spam carries that warning, with what to do next, until a later email to that address finishes delivered or the address changes.
Each email is in the `COMM-007` stream as an outbound email with its author, recipient and state.
Nothing is retried automatically: the desk sends again, or for a booking link revokes it and makes a new offer.

title: Timesheets and payroll export
acceptance: A fixture builds a 44-hour week, approves it, and checks the overtime split and the Gusto and QuickBooks Payroll exports; a subcontractor's total appears only in the 1099 export.
A workweek is seven local days in the business time zone from the owner's week-start day (Monday unless the owner sets another; fixed once any timesheet is approved).

Each closed shift counts its whole minutes (`COST-001` rounding) on the local day it started, including a shift that runs past midnight; job and travel timer minutes are shown beside it, and paid hours are the shift (clock) time.

When the owner sets a state rule, minutes past the "after" hours in a day are overtime and minutes past the optional "double after" hours are double time (quarter-hour settings, double after overtime); then, day by day in order, regular minutes beyond 40 hours in the workweek become overtime.
Seventh-day and other state rules are not applied.
Hours are each bucket's minutes / 60, rounded half up to two decimals, so rounded buckets can differ from the rounded total by 0.01.
A timesheet is flagged when it holds any overtime or double time.

title: Estimate versus actual job costing
acceptance: A fixture runs a job quoted at $1,850 with estimated 41% margin through recorded time, materials and an expense, and checks actual cost and a 46% margin to the cent.
Revenue is the latest person-approved invoice revision's subtotal before tax, else the accepted quote's subtotal.
The estimated cost is each accepted line's unit cost (kept when the line was priced from the price book, `MONEY-003, MONEY-006`) × its quantity; a line without one counts at $0.00 and is named.

Actual labor is every travel and on-job entry (`COST-001`) at its whole minutes × that technician's loaded cost per hour ÷ 60; materials are the price-book materials recorded on the job at the item's unit cost now, beyond what the job's own purchase orders received (`STOCK-002`), whose received lines count at the order's unit cost; expenses and subcontractors are `COST-003`'s amounts, subcontractor bills apart.
Each product is rounded half up to the cent; a margin is (revenue − cost) ÷ revenue as a percentage to one decimal, rounded half up, and the difference from estimate is in dollars and margin points.
The owner sets each technician's loaded cost per hour; like every cost it is a margin figure, read only by roles that read reports (`MONEY-003, MONEY-006`).

Reports take the jobs completed in a period (by local completion date, bounds inclusive) and roll them up by job type (the category of the job's first price-book line, else Uncategorized) and by technician (their minutes, labor cost and the jobs they recorded time on).

title: Live margin warnings
acceptance: A fixture records time past the threshold and checks one warning to each of the two people, and no repeat for the same crossing.

The owner sets, on the business, a cost threshold (warn when actual cost reaches this percentage of the estimate) and a margin floor (warn when projected margin falls below this percentage); either can be blank, meaning off.

A warning is kept once per job, kind and setting, so the same crossing never repeats; changing a setting can warn again.

title: Recurring jobs
acceptance: A fixture creates a quarterly series, skips one visit, moves another, changes the rule from a date, and checks every generated visit.

The dispatcher or owner makes an open job repeat (series create action) from a first local date, at a visit start and end time with one technician, on a rule: every 1–52 weeks (on the first date's weekday), or every 1–52 months, or every year in named months, on a day of the month (the first date's unless given; a day the month lacks becomes its last day) or on the first to fourth or last given weekday of the month; intervals count from the rule's first date.
Dates are local dates in the business time zone.
The series may end on a date (inclusive).

Visits are booked for every occurrence through the earlier of that end and today plus the series' rolling horizon (7–730 days, 365 by default): at create and change, conflicts are reviewed under `GLOVE-05` as for one booking; after every later command the horizon rolls forward and the newly booked visits carry their conflicts unreviewed, named on the job timeline for review on Dispatch, and an occurrence that cannot be booked (for example an inactive technician) is recorded once on the series and named on the timeline.

title: Recurring occurrence changes
acceptance: Each visit is an ordinary visit carrying its rule revision and occurrence date: moving it (visit change action) or skipping it (visit cancel action, labelled skipped) leaves the series unchanged, and an occurrence that has a visit is never booked again.

Changing the series from a date (series change action, with a reason, not before its first date) starts a new rule revision there: visits on or after that date that are still booked and untouched (no arrival, never moved) are canceled with that reason and booked again under the new revision; earlier visits and moved, skipped, started or completed ones stay as they are.
Completing one visit leaves a recurring job open; a visit completes the job only once the series has an end date, has booked through it and no other visit of the job is booked.
The series' invoicing rule comes with `PLAN-005, PLAN-012, PLAN-013`, which carries it in its text and acceptance; until then a recurring job is invoiced as one job under `GLOVE-09`.

title: Purchase orders to suppliers
acceptance: A fixture raises a PO for a job, receives it in two parts, and checks stock and job cost.

The owner and office raise a purchase order (numbered PO-0001 on) to a named supplier (with an optional email) of 1 to 50 price-book materials, each at a quantity to a thousandth of its unit and the supplier's unit cost (the item's price-book cost unless given), delivered to one van or warehouse (`STOCK-001`), for stock or for one job; it changes only while a draft.

A draft order goes to the supplier in one of two ways, and the record and timeline say which: the owner or office emails it from Glove to the order's supplier address, or another address the person names, through the owner's connected email (`COMM-001, COMM-010, COMM-011, COMM-012, COMM-013, COMM-014, COMM-015, COMM-016, COMM-017, COMM-018` email send action with kind purchase order; the order then reads sent, naming the email, with the provider's reported outcome, where delivered means only that the supplier's mail server accepted it), or the person sends it outside Glove by email, the supplier's portal, phone or in person and records that method with the supplier's reference, which is recorded as sent with no delivery claim.
Glove has no supplier-portal connection.

Only a sent order is received, in one or more parts, each line at most what is still due; each part adds to the delivery location's stock as a stock move naming the order (and its job), and the order reads partly received until every line arrives.

A job's received lines count to its actual cost (`COST-004`) at the order's unit cost; a price-book material recorded on that job counts at its price-book cost only beyond the quantity the job's orders received of it, so nothing is costed twice.
A job order shows on the property history (`CUST-001`).
Unit costs are margin figures (`MONEY-003, MONEY-006`): purchase orders are read only by roles that read reports, never by technicians.

title: Technician commissions and bonuses
acceptance: A fixture applies a 5% sold-revenue rule and a $25 agreement spiff over a period and checks the totals in the payroll export.

The owner alone (acting for "admin") sets commission rules in payroll settings: a percent of sold revenue, a percent of completed revenue and a fixed spiff per agreement sold, each optional (percents from 0 to 99.99 with up to two decimals; the spiff in USD).

Each save is a rule version applying from a local date (today unless the owner gives one), replacing any version from that same date; a credited sale takes the version in force on its local date in the business time zone, so a later change never alters earlier earnings.
Rules apply to every technician.

Sold revenue is an accepted quote's accepted total before tax (the chosen option and add-ons after any `QUOTE-007, QUOTE-019` discount), credited to the technician the desk names as its seller when recording the acceptance, on the local date the acceptance was recorded; a quote accepted with no seller credits nobody.

Completed revenue is `REPORT-002, REPORT-004`'s technician revenue: an invoice's latest approved revision before tax, split equally among the technicians who completed the job's visits (the cent remainder to the first by name), on the local date of its first approval.
A spiff is credited to the technician the desk names when selling a `PLAN-002` agreement, on the local date it was sold.
Each credited sale's commission is its base × percent, rounded half up to the cent; totals are sums of those amounts.

title: Job, revenue, technician and lead reports
acceptance: A fixture builds a fixture month and checks each report's totals against the records and the CSV export; one filter per report (period, branch, technician, job type, source) narrows its totals correctly, and the sales-tax-collected report matches the invoices' tax by jurisdiction to the cent.
Every report takes a period of local dates in the business time zone, both ends included, and one filter, and answers as JSON or as a CSV of the same figures, read by the roles that read reports.

Revenue is an invoice's latest person-approved revision subtotal before tax, counted once and dated by the invoice's first approval; the revenue report gives it by month and by job type (the category of the job's first price-book line, else Uncategorized, as in `COST-004`), filtered by job type.

The technician report gives each technician's revenue (each such job's revenue split equally among the technicians who completed its visits, the cent remainder to the first by name), visits completed in the period, callbacks (a completed visit followed within 30 days by a new job at the same site) and their rate, and hours (their clocked shifts that began in the period, to a tenth of an hour), filtered by technician.

Lead-source conversion counts the requests made in the period by source (`BOOK-003`'s figures), filtered by source; the quote win rate is quotes accepted ÷ quotes answered (accepted or declined) in the period, with the won value, filtered by the request's source; job margins are `COST-004`'s period roll-up, filtered by job type.

The sales-tax report sums the tax on approved invoices by month in one row per branch and jurisdiction, from each invoice's frozen `MONEY-001, MONEY-004, MONEY-005` tax breakdown (an invoice approved before `MONEY-001, MONEY-004, MONEY-005`, which has no breakdown, reports its tax under the business's former single jurisdiction), and says its basis: tax on approved invoices, because Glove records no payments yet.
Percentages are to one decimal, rounded half up.

The branch filter (`TEAM-002, TEAM-004, TEAM-005`) narrows every report to one branch's records and the revenue report also gives revenue by branch; the agreements report is `PLAN-002`'s (agreements sold in the period by plan with their value, those active on the period's last day, and churn).

title: Quote writer from the request
acceptance: A fixture drafts a quote for a 15-year-old furnace request (model fake) and checks three options from the price book with reasons, under the held company policy, held as a draft until the named person approves.

title: Repeat-callback diagnosis
acceptance: A fixture raises a callback on a condenser with two prior visits and checks the prepared checklist cites both visits' readings.

A new job (from a quote or a service call, which can name the site's equipment) is a callback when a unit it names had a visit on another job completed within the 30 days before the job was made, counted on the server's received completion time, the window `REPORT-002, REPORT-004` counts callbacks in; the job carries that flag and its timeline says so.

The agent (or the owner or a dispatcher) prepares the checklist with the owner's model provider (`FIELD-006, FIELD-011`'s connection): Glove gathers the unit's record, manual, photos and every earlier completed visit on it (form readings with their ranges and out-of-range flags, refrigerant, notes, materials), oldest first, each visit and reading with a reference; the model gets the equipment and visit evidence and photo captions only, never customer names, contacts or addresses.

Every checklist step and part must cite references the pack holds, and Glove resolves each citation to the recorded reading; an answer that cites nothing or anything else is refused and nothing is kept.

The prepared checklist is labelled advisory (the licensed technician diagnoses and decides the work; it is not a safety certification), decides no work, and is read by the desk and the technicians assigned to the callback job.
